reconcile.connective: Gill reads Jesus' question as revealing two natures in one person: truly David's son by descent, yet David's Lord by a higher nature.

discrepancy.connective: The sharpest reading is Wilhelm Wrede's: Jesus posed this very question, he argued, because he himself was not in fact a descendant of David.

skeptic.name: William Wrede
skeptic.attribution: William Wrede (1859-1906), "Jesus als Davidssohn," in Vorträge und Studien (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1907), 147-77

excerpts.excerpt_text: David, whose son you say the Messiah is, speaks of him as one superior to himself; as Lord, and as his Lord: whence is he then his son? … Our Lord meant by this, to observe to them, that the Messiah was God, as well as man; that he was not merely the son of David, as was commonly received, or a mere man, but that he had a superior nature, in which he was David's Lord, and even Lord of all.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States the David's-son/David's-Lord puzzle from Mark 12:35-37 and resolves it via a two-natures Christology, the classic harmonization the contradiction claim denies is available.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714), on Mark 12:35
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this exact pericope, arguing the scribes taught truly that Messiah is David's son but failed to also teach he is David's Lord and Son of God — both hold together.
